deliverables.text: A Riemann sum for the total water volume that passed the gage during each design storm: stated interval width AND where inside each day the Hero placed that day's value (Appendix D states the time convention), the sum, the result converted to acre-feet, and a one-sentence statement of whether the sum over-estimates, under-estimates, or exactly reproduces the volume in the published record, and how the Hero knows which of the three it is.

For each design storm, a fitted discharge function Q(t) over the storm window, its indefinite integral written as a general antiderivative with the constant of integration shown, and the definite integral of Q(t) across the storm window evaluated by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — compared in acre-feet against the D1 Riemann sum for the same storm.

For each design storm, a shaded diagram and a computation of the area between the fitted Q(t) curve and the horizontal channel-capacity line, over the interval where the storm exceeds capacity, with the limits of integration stated and derived; then the same floodwater volume read straight off Appendix A's daily values, and an accounting for the difference between the two figures.

A 'floodwater safely managed' table for The Crest Standard and The Basin Standard across both design storms, in acre-feet and built from Appendix A's daily values, each option's shortfall shown separately, then an acre-feet-of-floodwater-safely-managed per one thousand dollars of appropriation figure for each option against the two bid prices, and a recommendation.

The Reach: Capacity and Flood-Frequency Record

balance.argument_a: Above channel capacity the two design storms carry 52,629 acre-feet of floodwater between them. The Crest Standard passes all but 7,323 acre-feet of it — four days across the two storms, and never short by more than 2,133 cfs, on 2019-02-24 when The Slammed Door's daily mean of 8,060 cfs rises above the 5,927 cfs the raised crown carries. It manages 45,306 acre-feet, 1.19227 acre-feet per $1,000 of appropriation, ahead of the Basin Standard on the board's own number, and it takes no land out of production. Duration still costs it nothing: The Long Guest ran 6 days above capacity and the raised crown carried every one of them, clipping only the tops.
balance.argument_b: The Crest Standard's protection is a wall, and a wall has an edge: on 2019-02-24 it was already 2,133 cfs short, and this gage's own published 1% annual-exceedance peak is 27,800 cfs, several times the 5,927 cfs the raised crown carries. The Basin Standard has no such edge — peak is free to it. It absorbed all 19,374 acre-feet of the very storm that beat the crest, and what it ran out of was room, only on the second storm, where it held 24,000 of 33,255 acre-feet. It manages 43,375 acre-feet, 1.14144 acre-feet per $1,000 — behind by less than the width of MA2, the one figure this case admits it invented, on a scoring number that counts acre-feet and is blind to the shape of a failure. And the line that decides it is a convention, not a measurement: set channel capacity one row up Appendix B's own rating, at 22.00 ft instead of 21.50 ft, and the Basin Standard wins the board's number outright (A 1.09728 vs B 1.10808, margin 0.98%).
balance.margin_basis: Both bids are priced at the same appropriation (MA1), so the board's scoring number — acre-feet safely managed per $1,000 — has the same denominator for both options and the comparison is decided entirely by the two real hydrographs and the two bids' sourced capacities. margin_pct is (better - worse) / better on that metric: (1.19227 - 1.14144) / 1.19227 = 4.26%. Every figure is reproducible by hand from Appendices A-D with no undisclosed step. Computed in cases/total-flow/sensitivity_model.py.
balance.twist_effect: The Twist prices the Crest Standard's central claim that duration is free. Under a 4-consecutive-day sustained-loading limit (MA4) the raised crown loses the last 2 days of The Long Guest — 2,162 cfs-days, or 4,288 acre-feet — and manages 41,018 instead of 45,306 acre-feet, 1.07943 per $1,000. The Basin Standard is untouched at 1.14144, because storage does not care how long the water takes to arrive, so THE TWIST FLIPS THE WINNER: Option B goes ahead by 5.43%. Nobody's vote is proved wrong — the base recommendation was A by 4.26% — but the room now has to argue about which of the two numbers it believes, which is the point.
balance.stability: Probe 5 sweeps the four stated Modeling Assumptions (FLEX in sensitivity_model.py). No dial flips the recommendation and none pushes the margin past SPEC section 2's 20% cap: MA1 (appropriation) is margin-invariant because both options share the denominator; MA2 (unavailable storage) moves the margin to 3.16% at -50% and 5.37% at +50%; MA3 (drawdown) has no effect because the real storms are 64 days apart; MA4 is twist-only. SAID IN THE OPEN, because it is the honest counterpart: the base margin of 4.26% is narrow, and the three quantities that actually decide the case are not in FLEX at all — the channel capacity (1,934 cfs, S5 at S4's minor flood stage), the Crest Standard's design discharge (5,927 cfs, S5 at 26.00 ft, which is Bid A's SCOPE and not a measurement), and the Basin Standard's authorized 25,000 acre-feet (S8, a statutory ceiling). Appendix F names the first two on the page as choices rather than measurements, and states that moving either moves the answer: at 22.00 ft the winner changes. That is the balance, and it is visible to a Hero from the packet alone. Stress-testing the cited values themselves is probe 6's job, not probe 5's.

facilitator.twist: The geotechnical report Nadia ordered comes back, and it is not about the crest at all — it is about what is underneath the levee. A raised crown holds a higher river, but it does not hold it forever: under sustained high water the foundation begins to pass water beneath the embankment, and the district's emergency plan takes the reach out of service after four consecutive days of continuous loading — four consecutive days with the creek above CHANNEL CAPACITY, which is what Background means by loading the levee, not four days above the raised crown's design discharge — no matter how high the crown is. The Crest Standard's whole argument was that duration is free. It is not.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The district's appropriation, and that both bids come in at it
modeling_assumptions.basis: The Marrow Bend Levee District is fictional and has no published budget. The figure is set so that each bid's scope is the right size of job against real unit costs: 2.50 miles of crest raise and armoring at the rate implied by S9 ($258M / 17 mi / 5,280 ft = about $2,874 per linear ft, for an average 5 ft raise across a 17-mile Corps program) is about $37.9M across the whole reach; two detention pools flooding roughly 3,100 acres of Illinois cropland at S10's $9,850 per acre is about $30.8M before embankments and outlet works. Public bodies publish a budget and bidders price a scope to it. The 4.50 ft in Bid A's scope line is that bid's scope, NOT a height derived from S9's rate: a small district buying 2.50 miles of work does not get a 17-mile program's unit price, and the case does not claim it does. What the S9 arithmetic establishes is only that a crest raise of this order across this reach is the right size of job for this appropriation.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: None on the recommendation. Both options are divided by the same appropriation, so it cancels out of the comparison. Flexed +/-50% in probe 5: margin unchanged at 4.26%.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Share of authorized detention capacity unavailable when a storm arrives
modeling_assumptions.basis: Detention structures lose capacity to sediment accumulation and may hold an antecedent pool at the onset of an event. These structures do not exist, so no measured figure can exist; 4% is a small, deliberately conservative reservation.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The one genuinely load-bearing assumption in the FLEX set. Flexed +/-50% (2.0% to 6.0%) in probe 5: margin moves 3.16% to 5.37%, Option A ahead throughout, no cap break. Even at 0% unavailable — the statutory maximum of 25,000 acre-feet, which MA2 cannot legally exceed — Option A is still ahead (1.19227 vs 1.16775, 2.06%), so this dial alone cannot decide the case for Option B. What can is the channel-capacity convention: see balance.stability.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Time for the detention structures' outlet works to draw a full pool down
modeling_assumptions.basis: Standard practice sizes a flood-detention outlet to empty the pool within days, not weeks, so the storage is ready for the next event.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: None. The two real design storms are 64 days apart at the gage, so any drawdown from 5 to 15 days leaves the storage fully available for the second storm. Flexed +/-50% in probe 5: margin unchanged.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The sustained-loading threshold used in Appendix F's projection
modeling_assumptions.value_used: 4 consecutive days on which the creek runs above channel capacity — "loading the levee" in the sense Background gives it, not the raised crown's own design discharge
modeling_assumptions.basis: The district's geotechnical report is a scenario device; no real report exists for a fictional reach. Sustained high water driving underseepage beneath an embankment is a real and well-documented levee failure mode, and the direction of the effect (it costs the rate-based option, not the storage-based one) follows from the physics, not from the author's preference.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not enter the base recommendation at all — evaluate() never reads MA4, so nothing in the primary metric reads it. It governs only the sustained-loading question raised later in the discussion.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Data cutoff for every still-moving figure
modeling_assumptions.basis: SPEC section 5 requires one stated 'as of' cutoff applied to every number tied to a still-changing entity. Illinois cropland values (S10), the USGS stage-discharge rating (S5, rating 31.0 as retrieved 2026-07-02), and the NWS flood-category stages (S4) all change over time. Every one is frozen at the date this case was researched, and none is refreshed independently of the others. The two hydrographs (S2, S3) and the 1924-2017 flood-frequency record (S6) are closed historical records and do not move.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: None on the arithmetic. It is what makes the case checkable: a future reader can re-fetch each source and see exactly what moved.

sensitivity_note: Flooding touches property and personal safety. The case is framed entirely as protection — acre-feet safely managed, never damage inflicted or lives lost — but flag it for any learner with recent flood experience before the discussion runs.
